title: Delete and Earn
hints: picking value v earns you v times its count, but permanently blocks v-1 and v+1 - where have you seen 'pick this, but not its immediate neighbor' before?
first collapse the input: build an array points[v] = v * (count of v in nums) for every value from 0 up to the max value present
now the problem is exactly House Robber on the points array, where adjacency means consecutive integer values, not adjacent list positions
run best(v) = max(best(v-1), best(v-2) + points[v]) across all values, rolling just the last two results forward
commonMistakes: treating adjacency as 'adjacent positions in nums' instead of 'consecutive integer values', which is the actual constraint
forgetting to multiply each value by its count when building the points array, and just summing raw values instead
not handling gaps in the value range (values that never appear should contribute 0, not be skipped in a way that breaks the recurrence)

content.problemStatement:
You're given a list of integers, `nums`. In one move you pick some value
present in the list, earn a number of points equal to that value
multiplied by how many times it appears, and then every element equal to
(value - 1) or (value + 1) anywhere in the list is removed, along with
all copies of the value you picked. You can repeat this any number of
times.

**Return the maximum total points you can earn.**
constraints: picking a value removes every occurrence of value-1 and value+1 from future picks
notes: all elements are the same value (earn value * count in one pick)
consecutive integers where every pick blocks its neighbors, similar to House Robber

optimal.space: O(maxValue) for the totals array, O(1) extra for the rolling House Robber pass
optimal.pattern: dynamic programming - collapse to totals per value, then apply the House Robber recurrence over consecutive integers

bruteForce.approach: try every subset of distinct values such that no two chosen values are adjacent integers, summing value*count for each, and take the max
bruteForce.time: O(2^k) where k is the number of distinct values
